claim: Basal skin cells in zebrafish larvae are sensitive to changes in the particular ionic composition of their surroundings after wounding, specifically the concentration of sodium chloride in the immediate vicinity of the wound.
source: We find that, in addition to sensing osmolarity, basal skin cells in zebrafish larvae are also sensitive to changes in the particular ionic composition of their surroundings after wounding, specifically the concentration of sodium chloride in the immediate vicinity of the wound.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing wound responses in different ionic solutions (Figure 2), showing differential responses to sodium chloride versus other osmolytes.

claim: The sodium chloride-specific wound detection mechanism is independent of cell swelling.
source: This sodium chloride-specific wound detection mechanism is independent of cell swelling, and instead is suggestive of a mechanism by which cells sense changes in the transepithelial electrical potential generated by the transport of sodium and chloride ions across the skin.
evidence: The manuscript provides volume measurements showing that cells in different isosmotic solutions swell comparably despite different wound responses (Figure 3).

claim: Electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization and migration of basal cells in their native epithelial context in vivo.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization and migration of basal cells in their native epithelial context in vivo, even overriding endogenous wound signaling.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing cell migration in response to applied electric fields (Figure 4C-E).

claim: Electric fields can override endogenous wound signaling in zebrafish epidermis.
source: we show that electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization and migration of basal cells in their native epithelial context in vivo, even overriding endogenous wound signaling.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that exogenous electric fields can redirect cell migration away from wounds (Figure 4F).

claim: Skin cells respond to both osmotic and electrical perturbations arising from tissue injury to mount a robust wound response.
source: This suggests that, in order to mount a robust wound response, skin cells respond to both osmotic and electrical perturbations arising from tissue injury.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing wound responses to osmotic changes and electrical stimulation, and discusses their combined role.

claim: The initial wound response in many tissues consists of rearrangements of the actomyosin cytoskeleton to form a contractile purse string that closes the wound in concert with protrusive actin structures that promote cell migration toward the injury.
source: The initial wound response in many tissues consists of rearrangements of the actomyosin cytoskeleton to form a contractile purse string that closes the wound in concert with protrusive actin structures that promote cell migration toward the injury and help cover the damaged area (Abreu-Blanco et al., 2012; Eming et al., 2014; Rothenberg and Fernandez-Gonzalez, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Internal signaling events including waves of calcium influx, hydrogen peroxide release, and purinergic signaling occur in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury.
source: Yet many internal signaling events—including waves of calcium influx, hydrogen peroxide release, and purinergic signaling—occur in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury, suggesting that there must be other mechanisms by which cells sense injury on a tissue-wide scale (Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Xu and Chisholm, 2011; Yin et al., 2007; Yoo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Interstitial fluid in saltwater fishes is hyposmotic relative to the environment, while in freshwater fishes it is hyperosmotic.
source: for example, interstitial fluid in saltwater fishes is hyposmotic relative to the environment, while in freshwater fishes it is hyperosmotic (Boisen et al., 2003; Potts, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transport of sodium and chloride ions is essential for maintaining the transepithelial potential (TEP) in different tissues.
source: Ion substitution and pharmacological inhibition of ion channels suggests that transport of sodium and chloride ions is essential for maintaining the TEP in different tissues (Dietz et al., 1967; McCaig and Robinson, 1982; Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The wound response in Xenopus laevis and Danio rerio larvae is inhibited when the composition of the external medium resembles that of interstitial fluid.
source: In Xenopus laevis (clawed frog) and Danio rerio (zebrafish) larvae, the wound response is inhibited when the composition of the external medium resembles that of interstitial fluid (Fuchigami et al., 2011; Gault et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell swelling due to osmotic shock following injury provides a physical, cell-autonomous cue of tissue damage in zebrafish epidermal cells.
source: in zebrafish epidermal cells, cell swelling due to osmotic shock following injury has been shown to provide a physical, cell-autonomous cue of tissue damage, and this cue is amplified and relayed to other cells with subsequent extracellular ATP release (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hypotonic shock can promote formation of lamellipodia.
source: hypotonic shock can promote formation of lamellipodia (Chen et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hypotonic shock can intrinsically stabilize a polarized actin cytoskeleton by increasing mechanical feedback through membrane tension.
source: hypotonic shock...can intrinsically stabilize a polarized actin cytoskeleton by increasing mechanical feedback through membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Electric currents have been directly measured emanating from wounds in many animal tissues in the early phase of wound healing, including adult zebrafish skin, rat cornea and skin, tails of newt and Xenopus tadpoles, bronchial epithelia of rhesus macaques, and human skin.
source: Electric currents have been directly measured emanating from wounds in many animal tissues in this early phase, including adult zebrafish skin, rat cornea and skin, tails of newt and Xenopus tadpoles, bronchial epithelia of rhesus macaques, and even human skin (Ferreira et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2012; Nawata, 2001; Reid et al., 2009; Reid et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The currents measured emanating from wounds are approximately 10-100 times stronger than regeneration or developmental currents in the same model systems.
source: The currents measured emanating from these wounds are ~10–100 times stronger than regeneration or developmental currents in the same model systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Reid et al., 2005; Robinson, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In rat cornea, pharmacological perturbations that increase or decrease the magnitude of the wound current also correspondingly increase or decrease the rate of wound closure.
source: In rat cornea, pharmacological perturbations that increase or decrease the magnitude of the wound current also correspondingly increase or decrease the rate of wound closure, suggesting that electrical currents may aid in healing (Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A wide variety of cell types migrate directionally in the presence of an electric field.
source: it has been observed that a wide variety of cell types migrate directionally in the presence of an electric field (Allen et al., 2013; Riding and Pullar, 2016; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most cells appear to be responsive not to the magnitude of the electric field per se (in V/cm), but rather to the current density in their surroundings (in mA/cm2).
source: Importantly, most cells appear to be responsive not to the magnitude of the electric field per se (in V/cm), but rather to the current density in their surroundings (in mA/cm2), which is directly proportional to the electric field, scaled by the conductivity of the medium (Allen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Electric fields drag charged membrane proteins to one side of the cell by electrophoresis, with the resulting asymmetric protein distribution leading to cytoskeletal polarization, mediated by key signal transduction factors including phosphoinositide-3-kinase (PI3K).
source: a prevailing model is that electric fields drag charged membrane proteins to one side of the cell by electrophoresis, with the resulting asymmetric protein distribution leading to cytoskeletal polarization, mediated by key signal transduction factors including phosphoinositide-3-kinase (PI3K) (Allen et al., 2013; Sarkar et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The zebrafish larval epidermis is bilayered, with a superficial cell layer originating from the enveloping layer in early embryogenesis, and a basal cell layer that resides on a collagenous basal lamina and is specified by the ∆Np63 promoter.
source: The zebrafish larval epidermis is bilayered, with a superficial cell layer originating from the enveloping layer in early embryogenesis, and a basal cell layer that resides on a collagenous basal lamina and is specified by the ∆Np63 promoter (Bakkers et al., 2002; Le Guellec et al., 2004; Rasmussen et al., 2015; Sonawane et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: External culture medium for zebrafish has an osmolarity of about 10 mOsmol/l while the osmolarity of interstitial fluid inside the fish is estimated to be about 270-300 mOsmol/l.
source: external culture medium has an osmolarity of about 10 mOsmol/l while the osmolarity of interstitial fluid inside the fish is estimated to be about 270–300 mOsmol/l (Boisen et al., 2003; Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Within seconds after injury, the basal cell layer reacts to tissue damage primarily by active cell migration while the superficial layer reacts by purse string contraction around the wound.
source: Previous work in zebrafish has shown that, within seconds after injury, the basal cell layer reacts to tissue damage primarily by active cell migration while the superficial layer reacts by purse string contraction around the wound (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lacerated tissue rapidly reorganized and contracted around the wound site over a period of about 15-20 min.
source: We found that lacerated tissue rapidly reorganized and contracted around the wound site over a period of about 15–20 min (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Within two minutes of injury, actin polarized with significant accumulation of LifeAct-labeled filamentous structures on the wound-facing edges of the cell.
source: Within two minutes of injury, actin polarized with significant accumulation of LifeAct-labeled filamentous structures on the wound-facing edges of the cell, and the formerly static cell boundary began to rapidly protrude and retract on a sub-minute timescale, reminiscent of actin ruffling (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and video 2.

claim: Laceration prompted a stronger cell migration response within the first 5 min of injury compared with tail transection.
source: Interestingly, laceration prompted a stronger cell migration response within the first 5 min of injury compared with tail transection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Laceration injury induces intense and rapid propagation of increased calcium levels throughout the tailfin.
source: Consistent with observations from other model systems and wounding methods, we found intense and rapid propagation of increased calcium levels throughout the tailfin (Figure 1F; Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1F and video 4.

claim: The calcium wave propagated about five times faster than the cell migration wave (200 µm/min vs. 40 µm/min).
source: This calcium wave propagated about five times faster than the cell migration wave (200 µm/min vs. 40 µm/min, Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Cell movement is not directly triggered or regulated by the increase in calcium, though calcium may indirectly promote wound-induced migration by functioning as a permissive cue.
source: This suggests that cell movement is not directly triggered or regulated by the increase in calcium, though calcium may indirectly promote wound-induced migration by functioning as a permissive cue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that calcium waves propagate much faster than migration waves (Figure 1G-H).

claim: Larvae wounded in isosmotic sodium chloride had a markedly reduced wound response compared to larvae in E3 (hypotonic treatment).
source: Larvae wounded in isosmotic sodium chloride had a markedly reduced wound response compared to larvae in E3 (hypotonic treatment), as measured by average basal cell speed over time (Figure 2A, compare red with black trace).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sodium chloride had a uniquely strong inhibitory effect on wound response compared to other isosmotic treatments (choline chloride, sodium gluconate, potassium chloride, or sorbitol).
source: We found that, although all isosmotic treatments did reduce average cell speed, sodium chloride had a uniquely strong inhibitory effect (Figure 2A, compare red with other traces; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in magnitudes of the first principal component between sodium chloride treatment and all other treatments was statistically significant (p<0.001).
source: The difference in magnitudes of the first principal component between sodium chloride treatment and all other treatments was statistically significant (p<0.001, one-way fixed-effects Welch's ANOVA F(6, 19)=130.9, with Games-Powell post-hoc tests)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a striking lack of cytoskeletal reorganization in response to wounding in isosmotic sodium chloride, with the exception of the immediate vicinity around the wound.
source: Looking more closely at the dynamics of the cytoskeleton in the basal cell layer, we noticed that—with the exception of the immediate vicinity around the wound—there was a striking lack of cytoskeletal reorganization in response to wounding in isosmotic sodium chloride (Figure 2C; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C and video 1.

claim: LifeAct intensity increased in all isosmotic treatments except sodium chloride.
source: This analysis revealed that LifeAct intensity increased (often due to formation of lamellipodia) in all isosmotic treatments except sodium chloride, which did not induce any measurable cytoskeletal response at equivalent positions relative to the wound (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The specific inhibitory effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is independent of the anesthetic used in the experiments.
source: the wound response in larvae immobilized by alpha-bungarotoxin in isosmotic sodium chloride was nearly identical to the response of larvae treated with Tricaine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting the specific inhibitory effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is independent of the anesthetic used in the experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: When isosmotic sodium chloride media was present on only the tailfin, the wound response was identical to when the entire larva was immersed in that media.
source: When isosmotic sodium chloride media was present on only the tailfin, the wound response was identical to when the entire larva was immersed in that media (Figure 2G, compare red and pink traces).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-chamber device experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Only the local ionic environment regulates the wound response.
source: Moreover, when hyposmotic media was present only on the tailfin, the wound response was similar to that observed with uniformly applied hyposmotic media (Figure 2G, compare black and gray traces), suggesting that only the local ionic environment regulates the wound response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-chamber device experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Basal cells near the wound swelled dramatically within 90 s after wounding in hyposmotic media.
source: We found that basal cells near the wound swelled dramatically within 90 s after wounding in hyposmotic media (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Basal cell clusters from larvae wounded in hyposmotic media swelled by 50% of their initial volume on average and gradually shrank over 15 min.
source: This revealed that basal cell clusters from larvae wounded in hyposmotic media swelled by 50% of their initial volume on average and gradually shrank over 15 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by volume measurements over time (Figure 3B).

claim: Basal cell clusters from larvae wounded in isosmotic media of any composition increased in volume only slightly, with cells in sodium gluconate swelling the most—an increase of less than 6% on average.
source: In contrast, basal cell clusters from larvae wounded in isosmotic media of any composition increased in volume only slightly, with cells in sodium gluconate swelling the most—an increase of less than 6% on average.
evidence: The claim is supported by volume measurements (Figure 3B).

claim: For isosmotic media containing sodium chloride or choline chloride, the cellular volume change over 90 s post-wounding was not statistically significant.
source: For isosmotic media containing sodium chloride or choline chloride, the cellular volume change over this time frame was not statistically significant, nor was the magnitude of volume change in these media statistically distinguishable from that for cells on unwounded fish (p<0.05, two-sided t-tests on the paired average volume difference from each larva).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of volume measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: A linear relationship (r2 = 0.95) was observed between initial volume change and degree of cell migration for the four conditions in which the concentration of sodium chloride was varied.
source: A linear relationship (r2 = 0.95) was observed between initial volume change and degree of cell migration for the four conditions in which the concentration of sodium chloride was varied (Figure 3F)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cells exposed to isosmotic salts other than sodium chloride moved substantially more than would be expected based solely on their volume change.
source: while the conditions in which different salts were used did not follow this same linear relationship. Instead, cells exposed to isosmotic salts other than sodium chloride moved substantially more than would be expected based solely on their volume change.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of volume change and migration data (Figure 3F).

claim: Cells situated between the two electrodes rapidly polarized their actin cytoskeletons and migrated in the direction of the cathode, changing direction when the polarity of the electric field was reversed.
source: We observed that cells situated between the two electrodes rapidly polarized their actin cytoskeletons and migrated in the direction of the cathode, changing direction when the polarity of the electric field was reversed (Figure 4C–D; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4C-D and video 1.

claim: The directed movement of cells toward the cathode persisted regardless of whether the cathode was initially at the anterior or posterior electrode.
source: The directed movement of cells toward the cathode persisted regardless of whether the cathode was initially at the anterior or posterior electrode (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Within the native tissue context, electric fields are sufficient to induce and guide cell migration.
source: This suggests that, within the native tissue context, electric fields are sufficient to induce and guide cell migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of cell migration in response to applied electric fields (Figure 4C-E).

claim: In all larvae tested with exogenous electric fields opposing wound-induced fields, cells were dramatically slower in the presence of the exogenous electric field, and some cells even moved away from the wound toward the inserted cathode.
source: In all larvae tested, cells were dramatically slower in the presence of the exogenous electric field, and some cells even moved away from the wound toward the inserted cathode, which was never observed in unstimulated larvae (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Exogenous electric fields are sufficient to override the wound response of skin cells in a living animal.
source: This demonstrates that, in addition to guiding cells in the absence of wound stimuli, exogenous electric fields are sufficient to override the wound response of skin cells in a living animal.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There are at least two distinct ways in which epidermal cells detect tissue injury through changes in their external ionic environment.
source: Our results suggest that there are at least two distinct ways in which epidermal cells detect tissue injury through changes in their external ionic environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing osmotic and ion-specific responses.

claim: Mixing of interstitial fluid with dilute external media causes cells to swell, which prompts a migratory response.
source: First, mixing of interstitial fluid with dilute external media causes cells to swell, which prompts a migratory response, as has been previously shown (Enyedi et al., 2016; Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by volume measurements in this study.

claim: Fluid mixing specifically reduces the concentration of sodium and chloride ions around cells, which is sufficient to prompt actin polarization in basal epidermal cells near wounds, independent of cell swelling or any change in environmental osmolarity.
source: Second, this fluid mixing specifically reduces the concentration of sodium and chloride ions around cells, which we demonstrated is sufficient to prompt actin polarization in basal epidermal cells near wounds, independent of cell swelling or any change in environmental osmolarity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing actin polarization in different ionic conditions (Figure 2).

claim: One mechanism for cells to detect wounds that would be consistent with the osmolarity-independent effect of sodium chloride is through direct detection of electric fields arising from ion transport across the epidermis.
source: One mechanism for cells to detect wounds that would be consistent with this osmolarity-independent effect of sodium chloride is through direct detection of electric fields arising from ion transport across the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the experimental observations and theoretical considerations.

claim: Sodium and chloride are the predominant ions in both the interstitial fluids and external environments of freshwater fishes.
source: Sodium and chloride are the predominant ions in both the interstitial fluids and external environments of freshwater fishes, and these ions must be actively and continually absorbed from the environment to counteract leakage through tight junctions and urine (Kirschner, 2004; Potts, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TEPs have been measured in a variety of freshwater fish species, including trout, goldfish, and killifish, as well as in freshwater invertebrates like crayfish.
source: TEPs have been measured in a variety of freshwater fish species, including trout, goldfish, and killifish, as well as in freshwater invertebrates like crayfish (Eddy, 1975; Kerstetter et al., 1970; McWilliams and Potts, 1978; Wood and Grosell, 2008; Zare and Greenaway, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When the skin is breached, the established TEP will be short-circuited, leading to electrical potential gradients within the skin, which generate electric fields whose orientation will depend on the relative position of the wound.
source: And as shown in Figure 4A, when the skin is breached, the established TEP will be short-circuited, leading to electrical potential gradients within the skin, which generate electric fields whose orientation will depend on the relative position of the wound (Reid and Zhao, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical considerations illustrated in Figure 4A and supported by a citation.

claim: An electric field is sufficient to direct cell movement in vivo in the absence of other wound cues, and can even override endogenous wound cues at the same timescale as the normal wound response.
source: we have shown that an electric field is sufficient to direct cell movement in vivo in the absence of other wound cues, and can even override endogenous wound cues at the same timescale as the normal wound response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Electric currents have been directly measured in the external environment just outside of a wound in several model systems, including ex vivo wounded rat cornea, newt and tadpole tail amputation, and wounds in human skin.
source: Complementary to our electrical perturbation experiments in vivo, electric currents have been directly measured in the external environment just outside of a wound in several model systems, including ex vivo wounded rat cornea, newt and tadpole tail amputation, and even wounds in human skin (Ferreira et al., 2016; Nawata, 2001; Reid et al., 2009; Reid et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Early wound currents fall in the range of 5-500 µA/cm2, three orders of magnitude lower than the applied currents that cultured cells can respond to.
source: Paradoxically, these early wound currents fall in the range of 5–500 µA/cm2, three orders of magnitude lower than the applied currents that cultured cells can respond to Allen et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2011.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The physiological currents to which cells respond in vivo are restricted to small intercellular spaces, so the effective cross-sectional area through which current passes is small, and the current density within those spaces is large.
source: We believe that the most parsimonious explanation for this discrepancy is that the physiological currents to which cells respond in vivo are restricted to small intercellular spaces, so the effective cross-sectional area through which current passes is small, and the current density within those spaces is large (Robinson and Messerli, 2003).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the discrepancy between measured wound currents and cell sensitivity, supported by a citation.

claim: At least five types of ionocytes are responsible for maintaining ion homeostasis in zebrafish, each with a distinct complement of ion pumps, channels, and transporters, coupled by distinct electrochemical gradients.
source: At least five types of ionocytes are responsible for maintaining ion homeostasis in zebrafish, each with a distinct complement of ion pumps, channels, and transporters, coupled by distinct electrochemical gradients (Guh et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Teleosts do not have a homolog to the amiloride-sensitive sodium channel implicated in establishing the TEP in frog skin.
source: for example, teleosts do not have a homolog to the amiloride-sensitive sodium channel implicated in establishing the TEP in frog skin, and the channel responsible for sodium uptake from the external environment remains unknown (Venkatesh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Treatment of larvae with isotonic KCl elicited a similar wound response to other non-NaCl osmolytes, despite the strong effect KCl generally has on transmembrane potential.
source: Our results argue against a model in which this is accomplished primarily through changes in transmembrane potential: treatment of larvae with isotonic KCl elicited a similar wound response to other non-NaCl osmolytes, despite the strong effect KCl generally has on transmembrane potential (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In culture, basal epidermal skin cells from fish respond to electric fields through an electrophoretic mechanism, in which an unidentified membrane-bound protein (or proteins) is dragged by electrophoresis to one side of the cell, promoting cytoskeletal polarization and initiation or redirection of motility through a primary PI3K-dependent pathway and secondary myosin II-dependent pathway.
source: In culture, basal epidermal skin cells from fish respond to electric fields through an electrophoretic mechanism, in which an unidentified membrane-bound protein (or proteins) is dragged by electrophoresis to one side of the cell, promoting cytoskeletal polarization and initiation or redirection of motility through a primary PI3K-dependent pathway and secondary myosin II-dependent pathway (Allen et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Calcium dynamics are not required for sensing electric fields in cultured fish basal cells.
source: Although calcium dynamics are not required for sensing electric fields in cultured fish basal cells (Allen et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Electric fields are an attractive physical cue for wound detection because they are intrinsically directional, providing a mechanism to rapidly coordinate cell migration toward a wound at the spatial scales of tissue.
source: Electric fields are an attractive physical cue for wound detection because they are intrinsically directional, providing a mechanism to rapidly coordinate cell migration toward a wound at the spatial scales of tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the properties of electric fields.

claim: Changes in osmolarity and cell swelling do not encode directional information; these cues can initiate a wound response but must be coupled with an additional spatial cue in order to orient cell movement appropriately.
source: In contrast, changes in osmolarity and cell swelling do not encode directional information; these cues can initiate a wound response but must be coupled with an additional spatial cue in order to orient cell movement appropriately.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the properties of osmotic cues.

claim: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin, and human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP.
source: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin, and human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP, suggesting that electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans (Foulds and Barker, 1983; Knowles et al., 1981; Reid et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans.
source: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin, and human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP, suggesting that electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans (Foulds and Barker, 1983; Knowles et al., 1981; Reid et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of electric currents in human wounds and TEP in human tissues.

claim: Zebrafish are an ideal model system to further interrogate how cells respond to electric fields in physiological contexts.
source: Our direct observation of actin polarization in response to electric fields in vivo at rapid timescales of 5–10 min bridges the gap between detailed mechanistic studies in cell culture and functional studies in tissues, and suggests that zebrafish are an ideal model system to further interrogate how cells respond to electric fields in physiological contexts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results demonstrating electric field responses in zebrafish.
